title: When a balance is marked by several Reward Codes, the most recent marking event takes the whole attribution
content:
A.2.2.9.1.2.1.1.2.1 describes the Ethereum Mainnet Tracking Methodology — the Reward Code passed as a parameter when depositing USDS into the Sky Savings Rate or Token Rewards contracts, combined with withdrawal data and processed by Operational GovOps into net deposits — and then resolves the conflict case: "Where a balance has been marked with more than one Reward Code, the balance is attributed to the Reward Code specified in the **most recent marking event**."

This is last-touch attribution, and it has strong competitive consequences. Attribution is winner-take-all rather than shared, so there is no partial credit for the Integrator that originally acquired a deposit. And because the ten-year eligibility window (A.2.2.9.1.2.1.1.2.5) attaches to the marking event, a later marking transfers a claim that could have run for years.

The result is a contestable market in existing balances. An Integrator can grow revenue either by attracting new USDS or by inducing existing holders to re-transact through its own frontend — the second being cheaper. That keeps Integrators competing for users continuously rather than collecting rent on a one-time acquisition, but it also spends real resources moving balances that were already in the system.

The rule's virtue is that it is unambiguous and computable from on-chain data, which matters far more than fairness for a mechanism Operational GovOps must settle monthly across many Agents. Proportional or first-touch attribution would require history reconstruction and invite disputes; last-touch needs only the latest event.
description: Last-touch attribution makes reward claims winner-take-all and displaceable: a competing Integrator can capture a rival's ten-year claim by triggering a fresh marking event.
